lead: A point inside a machine part rarely feels a single stress: bending, torsion and axial load combine into three principal stresses, but a tensile test gives only one strength. A theory of failure turns the combined state into one equivalent stress that can be compared with the yield strength (ductile material) or the ultimate strength (brittle material). Shafts, brackets, pressure vessels and crank pins are all sized this way.
prereq: You need: principal stresses from combined loading and the factor of safety (see Combined and eccentric loading; principal stresses, and Factor of safety and design codes).

blocks.text: At a point, choose axes so that the shear stresses vanish. The normal stresses left are the principal stresses, ordered σ<sub>1</sub> ≥ σ<sub>2</sub> ≥ σ<sub>3</sub>, with tension positive and compression negative. The equivalent stress σ<sub>eq</sub> is the single uniaxial stress that would bring the tensile test bar to the same state of failure as the real combined stresses.

A ductile material fails by yielding, so it is checked against S<sub>yt</sub>. A brittle material fails by fracture, so it is checked against S<sub>ut</sub> in tension and S<sub>uc</sub> in compression. With a factor of safety n:

σ<sub>eq</sub> is the equivalent stress in MPa; S<sub>yt</sub> is the tensile yield strength; S<sub>ut</sub> is the ultimate tensile strength; S<sub>uc</sub> is the ultimate compressive strength (all in MPa); n is the factor of safety, a pure number.
Each theory names a different cause of failure. ν is Poisson's ratio (about 0.3 for steel); S<sub>sy</sub> is the shear yield strength the theory predicts.

head: Theory
Safe when
Use for
rows: σ<sub>1</sub> ≤ S<sub>ut</sub>/n in tension and |σ<sub>3</sub>| ≤ S<sub>uc</sub>/n in compression
σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> ≤ S<sub>yt</sub>/n, that is τ<sub>max</sub> ≤ S<sub>sy</sub>/n with S<sub>sy</sub> = 0.5S<sub>yt</sub>

blocks.text: Hydrostatic stress (equal on all three planes) changes volume but not shape and does not make a ductile metal yield; only the distortion energy theory leaves it out completely, which is why it fits ductile tests best. Coulomb–Mohr with equal strengths S becomes σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> ≤ S/n, which is Tresca, not Rankine.

In plane stress the Tresca safe region is a hexagon inside the von Mises ellipse, which passes through the same six corners, so Tresca is the safer of the two. The gap is largest in pure shear: 0.5S<sub>yt</sub> against 0.577S<sub>yt</sub>, about 15 %. The figure draws both, to scale, for the first worked example.

Choice rule: ductile steel, von Mises (most codes) or Tresca for a quick, safe answer; brittle cast iron, Rankine for mainly tensile stresses and Coulomb–Mohr when tension and compression both act. Repeated loading needs a separate check (see fatigue and the S–N curve).

sections.h3: Working forms for plane stress and shafts

blocks.text: σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub> and τ<sub>xy</sub> are the plane stresses in MPa (Mohr's circle).
Put into von Mises, the roots cancel:
A solid shaft of diameter d under moment M and torque T has σ<sub>x</sub> = 32M/(πd³), σ<sub>y</sub> = 0 and τ<sub>xy</sub> = 16T/(πd³), which gives:
Tresca: τmax = 16√(M² + T²)/(πd³) ≤ 0.5Syt/n von Mises: σeq = 16√(4M² + 3T²)/(πd³) ≤ Syt/n
M and T in N·mm, d in mm. √(M² + T²) is the equivalent twisting moment T<sub>e</sub>, used again in Shafts under bending, torsion and axial loads.

figure.caption: The three principal stresses enter a material-type decision. Ductile materials go to Tresca or von Mises; brittle materials go to Rankine or Coulomb–Mohr. Each path ends in one equivalent stress compared with the allowable strength.

spec.title: Choosing a failure theory
spec.aria: A flow chart from the three principal stresses through a material-type decision into the brittle or ductile theory, ending in one equivalent stress checked against the allowable strength.

examples.question: A steel shaft has S<sub>yt</sub> = 400 MPa. At its critical point σ<sub>x</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 40 MPa and τ<sub>xy</sub> = 60 MPa; the third principal stress is zero. Find the principal stresses, then the factor of safety by the maximum shear stress (Tresca) and distortion energy (von Mises) theories.
steps: Centre of Mohr's circle: (σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>)/2 = (100 + 40)/2 = 70 MPa.
In-plane principal stresses: 70 + 67.08 = 137.08 MPa and 70 − 67.08 = 2.92 MPa. With the zero stress, σ<sub>1</sub> = 137.08 MPa, σ<sub>2</sub> = 2.92 MPa, σ<sub>3</sub> = 0.
examples.answer: σ<sub>1</sub> = 137.08 MPa, σ<sub>2</sub> = 2.92 MPa, σ<sub>3</sub> = 0; n = 2.92 by Tresca and 2.95 by von Mises. They agree closely because the point sits near a corner the hexagon and ellipse share.

examples.question: A solid shaft of plain carbon steel (S<sub>yt</sub> = 380 MPa) carries a bending moment M = 1000 N·m and a torque T = 1500 N·m at the same section. Using a factor of safety of 2.5, find the shaft diameter by the maximum shear stress theory and by the distortion energy theory, and choose a size.
steps: Units: M = 1.0 × 10⁶ N·mm and T = 1.5 × 10⁶ N·mm.
Allowable stresses: shear 0.5 × 380/2.5 = 76 MPa (Tresca); normal 380/2.5 = 152 MPa (von Mises).
Choose the next standard size above both: d = 50 mm.
examples.answer: d = 49.43 mm (Tresca) and 47.89 mm (von Mises); a 50 mm shaft is safe by both. Tresca, the conservative theory, asks for the larger shaft.

traps: Setting σ<sub>3</sub> = 0 when an in-plane principal stress is negative: for 73 and −8 MPa, Tresca uses 73 − (−8) = 81 MPa, not 73.
Using S<sub>ut</sub> for a ductile material; it hides yielding.
Taking the shear yield strength as 0.5S<sub>yt</sub> in a von Mises answer. Von Mises gives S<sub>sy</sub> = 0.577S<sub>yt</sub>; 0.5S<sub>yt</sub> belongs to Tresca.
Using Rankine for ductile steel: it ignores shear yielding, most of all in torsion.
Entering a compressive σ<sub>3</sub> as positive in Coulomb–Mohr; keep it negative.

quiz.q: Why is Tresca called conservative compared with von Mises?
quiz.a: The hexagon lies inside the ellipse, so for the same stresses Tresca's σ<sub>1</sub> − σ<sub>3</sub> is never smaller than von Mises' σ<sub>eq</sub>, and n = S<sub>yt</sub>/σ<sub>eq</sub> is never larger.

quiz.q: A plane stress state has σ<sub>x</sub> = 80 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 20 MPa and τ<sub>xy</sub> = 40 MPa. Find the von Mises equivalent stress.
A cast iron bracket has S<sub>ut</sub> = 200 MPa and S<sub>uc</sub> = 600 MPa. Its principal stresses are 50 MPa and −150 MPa. Find n by Coulomb–Mohr and by Rankine, and say which governs.
quiz.a: Coulomb–Mohr: 1/n = 50/200 + 150/600 = 0.50, n = 2.0. Rankine: 200/50 = 600/150 = 4.0. Coulomb–Mohr governs because it counts both stresses together.

quiz.q: What shear yield strength does each ductile theory predict?
quiz.a: Tresca: S<sub>sy</sub> = 0.5S<sub>yt</sub>. Von Mises: S<sub>sy</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>/√3 = 0.577S<sub>yt</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does the plane stress von Mises formula contain the term 3τ<sub>xy</sub>²?
quiz.a: Putting the Mohr's circle values of σ<sub>1</sub> and σ<sub>2</sub> into σ<sub>1</sub>² − σ<sub>1</sub>σ<sub>2</sub> + σ<sub>2</sub>² cancels the roots and leaves 3τ<sub>xy</sub>² as the shear part.

quiz.q: A 40 mm shaft carries only a torque of 800 N·m and has S<sub>yt</sub> = 300 MPa. Find n by Tresca and by von Mises.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite element programs plot von Mises stress as a colour map over a whole part. Pressure-vessel codes use a Tresca-type stress intensity. Fibre composites need direction-dependent criteria such as Tsai–Wu. Search for 'von Mises yield surface' and 'modified Mohr theory'.
